title: Base64 That Decodes to Text
takeaway: Three features in run A/1 all fire on base64, and this figure shows what separates the third one: the strings A/1/1544 fires hardest on decode into readable source code and markup, while the best available decoding of A/1/2357's and A/1/2364's top examples is unreadable bytes. That turns a set of features that looked like a redundancy in the dictionary into a distinction the model is apparently making — between base64 that encodes text and base64 that does not.
walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Three rows, one per feature, all drawn from the same [[dictionary-learning]] run.

That run is A/1. In the paper's [[feature-notation]], "A/1/2357" means model A, run 1, feature number 2357.

Each row shows four [[top-dataset-examples]] for one feature — the windows of text, out of the sampled corpus, on which that feature fired hardest.

Every example is printed twice. The upper line is the raw base64 as the model read it. The boxed line underneath is what that base64 decodes to.

### How to read it

Orange shading behind a token is the feature's activation on that token, and darker means stronger. Bold marks the peak token. Each example is nine token-blocks wide: the peak token plus four tokens on either side.

The bracket under the string marks the substring that was decoded, and the tick points at where the peak token sits inside it.

Base64 carries $6$ bits per character, so four characters decode to $3$ bytes, and a decode only lines up on a group of four. The authors therefore tried different offsets and substrings and kept whichever output held the most printable ASCII characters. Hence the column header: *best* ASCII decoding. Bytes with no printable character are shown as `\xNN` escapes.

That choice is what gives the figure its force. If even the best available decoding is unreadable, the string is not encoded text.

### What it shows

Row 1 is the [[base64-feature]] A/1/2357, labelled "prefer letters". Row 2 is [[base64-digit-feature]] A/1/2364, "prefer digits".

Their boxes are almost entirely escapes — `z\x07\xe7|H\xbb\xbe\x00\xc8`, or `M\x9e\xaf\xe2-f`. Best case, these strings decode to bytes rather than to text.

Their shading also separates them from each other. A/1/2364 peaks on a lone digit — 9, 9, 5, 4 — with the surrounding letters left pale, while A/1/2357 peaks on a letter token in all four examples.

Row 3 is A/1/1544, "prefers encoded ASCII". Its boxes read `|\n        nul`, `xport def`, `-State1!0` and `>        </g` — fragments of source code and markup.

Its peak token is `ICAgICAg` in two of the four examples. Those eight characters decode to six spaces, the indentation of an encoded text file. The paper says that token was the first clue.

So the third feature is not a duplicate of the other two ([[multiple-features-for-one-context]]). It cuts base64 by what the base64 contains, which is the reading that makes [[feature-splitting]] look like refinement rather than a bug.

One limit: this compares four maximal examples per feature. It is a claim about the top of each feature's activation range, not about everywhere the features fire.

terms.definition: Labels the left column, which names the learned sparse-autoencoder feature whose examples are shown in that row. A feature here is a direction in the MLP activation space that the autoencoder learned, not a neuron of the transformer.

terms.term: Top Dataset Example, With Best ASCII Decoding (right column header)
terms.definition: Announces that each cell holds one of the corpus windows where the row's feature fired most strongly, printed above the most readable decoding the authors could extract from it. "Best" is literal: they searched over substrings and offsets and kept the decoding with the most printable ASCII characters.

The dictionary learning run these three features come from: model A, autoencoder run 1, which has 4,096 learned features. The paper's runs A/0 through A/5 hold the sparsity penalty fixed and increase the dictionary size.
The feature in row 1, the one the paper studies in depth earlier as its base64 case study. Within base64 contexts it fires preferentially on letters.

The feature in row 2, which fires preferentially on single digits inside base64. Its logit weights suppress digit continuations, which the paper attributes to the BPE tokenizer merging adjacent digits into one token.
The feature in row 3, and the one this figure exists to explain. The paper's reading is that it fires on base64 which encodes ASCII text.
The italic sub-label under A/1/2357, stating the paper's hypothesis for that feature. It marks a preference within base64 contexts, not a claim that the feature fires on letters generally.
The italic sub-label under A/1/2364. Its evidence is visible in the row: the strong shading sits on digit tokens and the letters around them stay pale.
The italic sub-label under A/1/1544, meaning it prefers base64 strings whose decoded bytes are readable ASCII text. This is the interpretation the figure is offered as evidence for.

An encoding that writes arbitrary bytes using the 64 characters [a-zA-Z0-9+/], packing 6 bits into each character. The model sees only these characters, never the bytes underneath, so any distinction between kinds of base64 has to be computed from the character sequence.

The byte values that correspond to ordinary readable characters — letters, digits, punctuation, space. A decoded byte outside that set has no character to print, so the figure prints its hex escape instead.

The dark-red items inside the decoding boxes, each standing for one decoded byte with no printable character, written as two hex digits. A box that is mostly escapes means the decoding produced binary, not text.
The feature's activation on that token, with darker orange meaning a larger activation. This is the paper's standard activation display, used throughout its feature visualizations.
The token in the window with the highest feature activation — the token the example was selected around. The paper's interpretability rubric refers to these as the "high-activation (bolded) tokens".
A token on which the feature is at or near zero. In row 2 these are the letters sitting next to the digit the feature actually responds to.

terms.term: Bracket and tick beneath a string
terms.definition: The bracket spans the substring that was fed to the decoder, and the tick drops from the peak token to the box, connecting the activation above to the decoding below. The bracket is usually shorter than the printed example because decoding needs a four-character-aligned window.
The bordered monospace box under each example holding the decoded output for the bracketed substring. Printable characters are dark, non-printable bytes appear as red escapes.

The peak token in two of A/1/1544's four examples, and the token that first suggested the ASCII interpretation to the authors. It decodes to six consecutive spaces, which is what indented source code looks like once encoded.
The peak token in A/1/1544's second example, sitting inside a stretch that decodes to "xport def". It is a two-character fragment of the encoding, not a unit with meaning of its own.
The peak token in A/1/1544's third example. It falls inside "LVN0YXRl", which decodes to "-State".
The peak token in all four of A/1/2357's examples, a capital letter. It is consistent with the row's "prefer letters" label, though the figure does not claim the feature is specific to the letter E.

terms.term: Row 1 and row 2 example strings (yegfnfEi7vgDI, /eqkllEjyFa65e, dtDcVfEytMoriKs, 2ilSLlfEvlE4011, /z6fj9Vjbncv, aReHHh9C3V84, 6Rwut5/aOib, mTZ6v4i1mR)
terms.definition: The eight top-activating windows for the letters feature and the digits feature. They read as arbitrary base64, and their decodings confirm it.
The four top-activating windows for A/1/1544. Each contains a run that decodes cleanly into text.

The four decoded fragments in row 3, which look like pieces of source code and markup — an escape sequence and "null", part of "export def...", a hyphenated identifier, and the close of an SVG group tag. They are fragments because the decoding starts mid-file, not at a token boundary of the original text.
A unit of the transformer's BPE vocabulary; the shaded blocks are tokens, not characters. This is why a single block can hold eight base64 characters (ICAgICAg) while another holds one digit.

numbers.meaning: Rows, one per feature. The paper found exactly three features in run A/1 that fire on base64, and the figure puts all three side by side because the question being answered is why there are three rather than one.

Top dataset examples shown per feature, for 12 examples in total. Four is a display choice, and it is also the figure's main evidential limit: "none of the top examples decode" is a statement about four windows apiece.
The feature indices inside run A/1. The numbers are arbitrary labels assigned by the autoencoder's initialization, and carry no ordering — 1544 is not earlier or more important than 2357.
Token blocks per example. The paper's visualization appendix says it displays a window of four tokens on each side of the selected token, so four plus the peak plus four.
Dictionary sizes for runs A/0, A/1 and A/2. The count of base64-specific features goes 1, then 3, then many across these runs, which is what feature splitting means in this case.
The single base64 feature in the 512-feature run, which appeared to fire on all tokens of base64 strings. The three features in this figure jointly cover roughly what that one feature covered.
Information carried by one base64 character, since the alphabet has 64 = 2^6 symbols. This is why decoding is only defined on groups of four characters.

The base64 block size: 4 x 6 = 24 bits = 3 bytes. Because of it, a decode attempt has to be aligned, so the authors sweep the alignment and keep the substring whose decoding has the most printable characters.

The size of the token ICAgICAg and of its decoding — two aligned blocks, giving six bytes that are all the space character. Six spaces in a row is a strong sign of indented text rather than random data.

The peak tokens across A/1/2364's four examples, all single digits. This is the visible evidence for the row's "prefer digits" label; the digits are single because the tokenizer would have merged two adjacent digits into one token.

The range of hex byte escapes appearing in the row 1 and row 2 decoding boxes (\x07, \xe7, \xbb, \xd0, \xf1, \xff, \x9f, \xdd and others). Each is a decoded byte with no printable ASCII character, and their density is the figure's measure of "this is not encoded text".
Ordinary base64 characters that happen to be digits, appearing in the raw example strings. They carry no numeric meaning — base64 uses 0-9 as 10 of its 64 symbols.
Decoded output characters in row 3's third box, not activations or indices. They are part of whatever text was encoded, which the fragment does not reveal in full.
